children.value: Define successful responses and failures before writing the UI.

GET reads and must not perform a requested mutation. PUT describes replacement and is idempotent by intended effect. PATCH describes a partial change and is not inherently idempotent. DELETE is idempotent by intended effect even if later responses differ. POST is not inherently idempotent; use an agreed idempotency key when retries could duplicate a purchase or job.

Use 200 for a successful body, 201 for creation (often with Location), 202 for accepted work that is not finished, and 204 for success without a body. A 304 is cache validation, not a JSON success body. Distinguish malformed input (400), missing/invalid authentication (401), insufficient permission (403), absence (404), conflicting current state (409), failed preconditions (412), semantically invalid content (422 under your API convention), throttling (429), and server failure (5xx). Avoid leaking stack traces, SQL or private resource existence.

Treat JSON as unknown. Check object shape, required fields, lengths, allowed enum values and cross-field rules. Reject or deliberately strip unknown keys; never pass unfiltered input into a database update. Client validation improves feedback; server validation enforces the contract. Limit body size and list size. Return stable error codes, safe messages and field paths; retain a request ID in server logs.

Offset pagination is simple but inserts can shift pages. Cursor pagination uses a stable total order, for example created_at plus unique id. Encode and validate both cursor values; scope the query to the authenticated owner on every page. Fetch limit + 1 to determine hasNextPage. Cursors are positions, not permission tokens. title: The event loop, tasks & microtasks
description: Predict execution order before running the code.

questions.answer: No. Its callback runs in a later task after the current execution and relevant microtasks. The delay is a scheduling threshold, not a deadline.

questions.question: Can microtasks delay the page?

facts: Promises do not create a separate JavaScript thread.
Microtasks queued by other microtasks are drained at the checkpoint.
Browser and Node.js host scheduling are not identical.

solutionNotes: No. Its callback runs in a later task after the current execution and relevant microtasks. The delay is a scheduling threshold, not a deadline.

-- parameter $1 is the authenticated owner.
select n.id, n.title, count(c.id) as comment_count
from notes n left join comments c on c.note_id = n.id
where n.owner_id = $1
group by n.id, n.title
order by n.id;

update inventory set available = available - 1
where id = $1 and available > 0
returning available;

create index notes_owner_created_id on notes(owner_id, created_at desc, id desc);

every affected index must be maintained alongside table changes, adding work and storage.

compiler options and inference should be checked with your project compiler."},"next":"ts-narrowing-never"} ## the idea

type annotations check a value but can broaden its apparent type. satisfies checks assignability while retaining the expression’s useful inferred type. as const prevents literal widening and gives object properties and array positions readonly types.

## why it matters

use satisfies for route maps, variant dictionaries and configuration objects. it is not a cast or a runtime validator. as const is also compile-time only: aliases can still refer to mutable runtime objects. template literal types combine string unions, making useful event and route contracts without runtime string validation.

## a practical example

```ts
type route = { path: string; private: boolean };
const routes = {
  notes: { path: "/notes", private: true },
  login: { path: "/login", private: false },
} as const satisfies record<string, route>;

type routename = keyof typeof routes; // "notes" | "login"
type event = `${routename}:opened`;
const event: event = "notes:opened";
const path = routes.notes.path; // "/notes"
```

## common mistakes

do not replace validation of dynamic configuration with satisfies. an assertion can hide an invalid object; satisfies reports a mismatch. excess-property checking is strongest on fresh literals and is not exact-object validation.
